questions.q: In a crontab line, what does `*/15 * * * *` mean for when the command runs?
options: Every 15 minutes, every hour, every day
15 times total, then it stops
Once, at 15 minutes past midnight
On the 15th day of every month
questions.explain: */15 in the minute field means every 15 minutes; with every other field left as *, the job runs every 15 minutes around the clock, every day.

questions.q: What's the key difference between a user's own crontab (edited with `crontab -e`) and a file in `/etc/cron.d/`?
options: A file in /etc/cron.d/ includes an extra field specifying which user the job runs as, while a user crontab always runs as that user
There is no difference; they behave identically
A user crontab supports more time fields than /etc/cron.d/
/etc/cron.d/ files can only run shell scripts, never binaries
questions.explain: A personal crontab always runs as the owning user. System crontab files under /etc/cron.d/ (and /etc/crontab) add an explicit user field so a job can run as a different account.

questions.q: Why is a systemd timer's service unit typically given `Type=oneshot`?
options: Because oneshot services run faster than normal services
Because oneshot is required for any unit paired with a timer
Because the service is expected to run once and exit, not stay running continuously
Because it prevents the service from ever failing
questions.explain: Type=oneshot tells systemd that the process will do its work and exit, rather than remain running — appropriate for a scheduled task like a nightly export.

questions.q: What does `Persistent=true` do in a `.timer` unit?
options: Prevents the timer from ever being disabled
Makes the timer run continuously instead of on a schedule
Saves the timer's output permanently to a log file
If the scheduled run was missed because the system was off, runs the job as soon as the system is back up
questions.explain: Persistent=true catches up on a missed scheduled run (e.g., the server was powered off at 2am) by triggering it once the system comes back online.

questions.q: Why are systemd timers generally easier to debug than cron jobs?
options: A timer's paired service logs through the normal systemd/journalctl path, giving a full history of runs and exit status; cron output is just mailed or dropped
Timers run faster than cron jobs
Timers don't require any configuration file
cron jobs cannot write any output at all
questions.explain: Because a timer triggers a real systemd service, that service's execution is logged through journald automatically — journalctl -u <service> shows every past run. cron, by contrast, mails output or discards it with no built-in run history.
